blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Collapses: Finesse Wireless and the Federal Circuit’s Renewed Policing of Infringement Proof
blogs.description: This post would examine the court’s most important holding: that a jury verdict cannot stand when the patentee’s infringement case depends on an expert who never clearly maps the accused system onto the claim limitations and instead offers internally contradictory testimony. The post would situate the opinion alongside cases like Johns Hopkins v. Datascope and explore how Finesse Wireless sharpens the line between permissible inferences and post hoc appellate reconstruction of an expert’s theory. It would also discuss practical implications for patent trial practice, especially in software and signal-processing cases built around diagrams, shorthand labels, and architecture documents.

blogs.title: Three Signals, Seven Multiplications, and No Infringement: What Finesse Wireless Says About Mathematical Claim Limitations
blogs.description: This post would focus on the ’775 patent and the court’s insistence that mathematical claim language be proved with precision. Although the panel declined to find prosecution-history surrender of systems using only two unique input signals, it still reversed because the patentee failed to show that the accused radios performed the seven specifically claimed multiplications. The post would analyze the court’s treatment of complex conjugates, modulus operations, and ‘distinct’ versus repeated multiplications, and argue that the decision reflects a broader trend toward demanding rigorous element-by-element proof for algorithmic and DSP-related patent claims.

blogs.title: A Narrow View of Prosecution Disclaimer, a Broad Demand for Trial Proof
blogs.description: This post would explore the tension in the opinion between claim-scope doctrine and sufficiency-of-the-evidence doctrine. On the one hand, the Federal Circuit rejected AT&T and Nokia’s argument that amendment from ‘two or three signals’ to ‘three signals’ clearly and unambiguously disavowed systems with only two unique inputs. On the other hand, the court still found no substantial evidence of infringement because the trial record never established that the accused products satisfied the exact multiplication requirements. The post would explain why the decision is notable for being relatively restrained on disclaimer while still being unforgiving on evidentiary gaps, and what that means for litigants deciding whether to fight over claim construction or over proof at trial.

blogs.title: Reversing the Verdict, Vacating $166 Million: The Fragility of Lump-Sum Damages After Total Infringement Failure
blogs.description: This post would analyze the damages implications of the decision. Because the panel reversed infringement on all asserted claims, it vacated the entire $166 million lump-sum award without reaching the district court’s damages rulings. The post would use the case to discuss the structural vulnerability of large patent verdicts that rest on a single unified infringement theory, especially where the same expert narrative supports both liability and damages. It would also consider what the opinion signals for post-trial strategy in the Eastern District of Texas and in Federal Circuit appeals where liability defects may render intensive damages disputes irrelevant.
